summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Screening carries an outing risk independent of Arkansas law. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud. Several governments responded: in April 2025 CNN reported advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens.

Facilities restrictions apply across a widening band of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans covering trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Arkansas enacted Act 619 on 11 April 2023, becoming the fourth state to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender; the Movement Advancement Project's February 2026 citations record the measure as HB 1156, a 2023 K-12 facility ban amended and extended in 2025. Enforcement elsewhere has produced arrest: in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Arkansas in its "Worst Policies In Effect" group alongside Alabama, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Ohio, Oklahoma, North Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming, one tier below the four states graded "Do Not Travel": Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. Idaho reached that grade after a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years, partially court-blocked but in force where no gender-neutral option exists; Kansas is graded over a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime. The assessment records the 2026 legislative season as continuing to degrade trans rights while federal policy drives nationwide trends.

Federal custody and federal enforcement present documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
tangentialFactors:
Arkansas sits one tier below the states carrying explicit "Do Not Travel" grades for trans people, so the risk profile is severe without being formally maximal; the distinction rests on grading rather than on a materially different legal category, and the July 2026 assessment notes the tiers move as legislatures act. Idaho's promotion to "Do Not Travel" followed a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years, and Kansas's followed a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime, both showing how quickly a state's grade can change within a single legislative season.

The national picture behind the Arkansas facility rule is uneven rather than uniform: bans on trans bathroom use apply in nine states and one territory in schools and some government buildings, additional states impose outright facility bans, and 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have none. Some states criminalise trans bathroom use in certain circumstances, and several states have moved on documents as well, including a February 2026 Kansas law barring changes to birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing mismatched documents.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned in 27 states nationally, with Arkansas among the states litigating over such a ban. Several federal measures in this area have been blocked or enjoined, so the operative position on care and on documents has shifted through the courts rather than settling.
localsOnly:
Arkansas was the first state to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, in 2021, after the legislature overrode the governor's veto; critics at the time called it the single most extreme anti-trans law to pass a state legislature. A federal judge enjoined the ban for "irreparable harm" to minors while litigation continued, and litigation over the 2021 care ban is still running.

State law has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981, a document rule that has outlasted the more recent legislative period. Arkansas's facility restriction, Act 619, took effect as a 2023 measure directed at K-12 schools and was amended and extended in 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state whether Arkansas's facility restriction reaches adults or public accommodations outside K-12 schools, so visitor exposure in restaurants, hotels, workplaces and government buildings in Arkansas is unresolved rather than established.

The precise scope of the 2025 amendment and extension of Act 619, and its current litigation status, are not sourced here; the July 2026 risk grading is a categorisation by an external assessor and carries no citation to a specific Arkansas enforcement action.

Arkansas driver's licence and state-issued ID marker rules are not covered by the sources provided. Whether Arkansas mirrors the federal birth-certificate position, and whether any state enforcement has followed from the federal redefinition of sex, remain unsourced.

No Arkansas-specific data on trans people in federal custody, on arrests under facility laws, or on state response to the December 2025 bounties directive appears in the inventory.
